Patients with se- rum-erythropoietin above 500 mU/mL and a good proba- bility of response to immunosuppressive therapy should be given antilymphocyte immunoglobulins with or with- out ciclosporin, or possibly ciclosporin alone.3,7 Those likely to have a poor response to immunosuppressants should be given treatment with azacitidine, decitabine, le- nalidomide, investigational agents, or considered for allo- geneic HSCT.3 Azacitidine or decitabine are also treat- ment options for patients with serious cytopenias; if not responsive, immunosuppressive therapy, investigational agents, or allogeneic HSCT can be tried.3 Lenalidomide is effective for patients with chromosome 5q deletions,8-10 and is recommended as first-line therapy in these pa- tients.3,7 The treatment of progressive or advanced myelodysplastic syndromes or those that have transformed to AML may involve intensive chemotherapy similar to that for AML (see p.652), but remission rates are lower,1,2,4,5 and relapse common.7 However, many patients are elderly with poor performance status, and are unable to tolerate intensive chemotherapy. They may be treated with supportive care and haematopoietic growth factors alone.7 Low-intensity chemotherapy such as azacitidine or decitabine may be tried in such patients,3 but has had limited success.2,4 Other antineoplastics and immunomodulating agents investigat- ed for use in myelodysplastic syndromes include amifos- tine, arsenic trioxide, thalidomide, and topotecan.2,4-7,11 Attempts to induce cellular differentiation have generally been disappointing.4 1.
